newsitem.title: POLAND: Poles part with their millions after money change.
newsitem.headline: Poles part with their millions after money change.

text.p: Poland Wednesday withdrew from circulation its old bank notes denominated in thousands and millions of zloty, ending a two-year transition to a manageable currency from one ravaged by past inflation.
On the first day of 1995, the country launched its so-called "denominacja" or redenomination, lopping four zeroes off the zloty so that 10,000 old zlotys became worth one new zloty.
New bank notes and coins were introduced, but old notes were only slowly phased out and, until now, a handful of cash could include an old million-zloty note and a new 100, both worth $35.
"We can say that the change was a success for the National Bank of Poland (NBP) and the whole banking system," central bank President Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz said last month.
"Everyone quite quickly got used to having two currencies over these two years and it was not so hard for many people as was initially feared," she told a news conference.

She said that by Dec. 10, about 95 percent of bank Notes were in new zlotys. Poles will be able to change old notes for the next 14 years, but the NBP chief said about 2 percent, mostly for small amounts, might not be recovered.
Despite a reassuring NBP advertising campaign before the change, opinion polls revealed widespread anxiety.
Old people worried they would not cope or could lose out badly from mistakes in circumstances where 30,000 old zlotys could buy a bottle of beer and 30,000 new ones a small car.
Some feared shops would use the chance to round up prices, although shopkeepers had to quote prices in old and new zlotys.

Gronkiewicz-Waltz said the reform had not pushed up inflation. In 1995, consumer prices fell by as much as eight percentage points and had declined further in 1996 to reach an annualized inflation rate of 19.1 percent in November.

The redenomination was a major step toward boosting confidence in the currency after frightening price rises during the dismantling of the communist system in 1989 and 1990, when people rushed to spend money before it lost value.

This inflation, at times exceeding 1,000 percent year-on-year, meant even poor Poles could ruefully call themselves millionaires -- the monthly average wage is now about 1,000 new zlotys or 10 million old ($350).
The reform allowed the reintroduction of Poland's cent, the grosz. Back came coins, rendered worthless in the 1980s, which are more durable and economical than paper money.
Commercial banks told Reuters that despite the adjustment costs of the switch, it had made operations easier.
"It has clearly helped a host of operations ... of course there were costs, but all in all in was worth it," said Marek Minarczuk, of Pekao SA bank's public relations department.
